newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. extends troops in Croatian enclave 6 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. extends troops in Croatian enclave 6 months.

text.p: The Security Council on Friday extended its mission in the Croatian enclave of Eastern Slavonia until the middle of 1997 and left open the option of U.N. personnel remaining until the end of the year.

The Serb-held enclave bordering the Yugoslav republic of Serbia is the last remaining Croatian area not under Zagreb's control. A U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) is preparing the province for a return to Croatian rule.

In a resolution adopted unanimously, the council said UNTAES, with 5,000 troops, would stay in the region until July 1, but the council said it might remain until the end of 1997 with a "restructured" presence even after Croatia is expected to assume control. Elections in the region are anticipated for April and Croatian envoys believe troops will begin to leave a month later if the area is peaceful.

The current extension does not expire until mid-January but Jacques Klein, the American diplomat who heads the mission, argued that its renewal had to take place as soon as possible to quell disputes in the region over the mandate.

Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman had wanted all troops out in January or March. But Germany and the United States, which negotiated the arrangement at the Dayton, Ohio, Balkan peace talks last year, insisted on an extented timetable.

Thousands of people were killed or expelled from the region that saw some of the worst fighting in a six-month war sparked by Croatia's bid for independence from ex-Yugoslavia in 1991. The city of Vukovar on the Danube was devastated.
The Dayton agreement also guaranteed 100,000 Croats driven out of the region the right to return, while Serbs who lived there when the war erupted could retain their homes.

The Croatian army recaptured two other Serb enclaves in blitz offensives in 1995, causing a Serb exodus. According to U.N. figures, 60,000 Serbs found refuge in Eastern Slavonia, while some 120,000 others fled to Bosnia and Yugoslavia.

UNTAES is to prepare Eastern Slavonia for reconciliation with Croatia, including economic rehabilitation, law and order, the return of refugees, construction of housing and the organisation of local elections before its mandate expires.
Friday's resolution urged Croatia and local Serbs to "avoid actions which could lead to refugee movements" and reaffirmed the right of all Croatians "to return to their homes of origin."

An unknown factor is how many Serbs will flee to Serbia after Croatia takes over. Peter Galbraith, the U.S. ambassador to Croatia, said last week that 20,000 Eastern Slavonia residents, most of them Serbs, have applied for Croatian citizenship. But no Croatian refugees have yet returned.
